pr_title: run permit plugins in the scheduling cycle
pr_body:

4. If you want *faster* PR reviews, read how: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md#best-practices-for-faster-reviews
5. If the PR is unfinished, see how to mark it: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md#marking-unfinished-pull-requests
-->

**What type of PR is this?**
/kind feature
/sig scheduling

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Scheduler framework permit plugins now run at the end of the scheduling cycle, after reserve plugins. Waiting on permit will remain in the beginning of the binding cycle.

This change guarantees the intuitive order in which permit plugins will be executed. If pod should wait on permit, then pod will be added to the waiting pods map before permit plugins are executed for another pod. This change removes subtle races between creation of and rejecting/allowing waiting pod and simplifies implementation of some potential permit plugins e.g. co-scheduling plugins.

- [x] split and move RunPermitPlugins to the scheduling cycle
- [x] fix and add new unit tests
- [x] document WaitOnPod
- [x] document buffered channel
- [x] fix integration tests
- [x] fix ete tests
- [x] update documentation of the snapshot lister

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #88179

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:

```release-note
Scheduler framework permit plugins now run at the end of the scheduling cycle, after reserve plugins. Waiting on permit will remain in the beginning of the binding cycle.
```

issue_context.title: Move scheduler's framework permit API to the scheduling cycle and wait in the binding cycle
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
I suggest moving execution of permit plugins and the creation of a waiting pod to the scheduling cycle, right after reservation, but keep waiting on a waiting pod's channel in the binding cycle.

- This way permit plugins will be executed sequentially and result of a previous permit plugin execution will be visible during a next execution.
- With this change it will be easier to reason about waiting pods and implementations of the permit plugins will be simpler and less buggy. For example this will make features like gang scheduling much easier to implement correctly. 
- It will also potentially allow to use `SnapshotSharedLister()` in the permit plugin.
- I suspect that execution of the permit plugin will not be very expensive in the most scenarios, so it is okay to move it to the scheduling cycle.

**Why is this needed**:
There are potential races when running a permit plugin that makes them hard to use, e.g.

1. permit plugin for pod A returns "Wait"
2. permit plugin for pod B reads currently waiting pods and allow some of them and return "Allowed"
3. pod A is added to the waiting pods and is never allowed

In general, the issue is that there is no way to know when a pod will become "waiting pod" after returning "Wait" from the plugin. This leads to races where some pods are allowed and then waiting pod arrives and is potentially never allowed.

/sig scheduling
comments:
A scheduling cycle blocks the next one. If we move execution of permit plugin to scheduling cycle, you have to run it in a goroutine as permit plugin is meant to perform conditional waiting. In that case, the benefits you listed doesn't sound fair:

> This way permit plugins will be executed sequentially and result of a previous permit plugin execution will be visible during a next execution.

Are you trying to say permit plugins for different pods will be executed sequentially? If so, as I mentioned above, permit plugin shouldn't block scheduling cycle, so you still need to assume permit plugins for a group of pods are running asynchronously.

> I suspect that execution of the permit plugin will not be very expensive in the most scenarios, so it is okay to move it to the scheduling cycle.

It's not related with cost of a permit plugin. It's that a permit plugin would wait, and the wait definitely shouldn't block the main scheduling goroutine.

> 1. permit plugin for pod A returns "Wait"
> 2. permit plugin for pod B reads currently waiting pods and allow some of them and return "Allowed"
> 3. pod A is added to the waiting pods and is never allowed

I didn't quite get this. Isn't that when permit plugins come to pod B, pod A is already in `waitingPod` (due to the lock on it), if at that moment, the permit plugin doesn't want to `Allow` pod A, then it's as expected, why are you concerning about pod A is never allowed? Or, are you trying to say: even pod A is handled ahead of pod B in the scheduling cycle, it's also _possible_ that, in binding cycles, pod B can happen before pod A?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b8e2b0d990ee0b780198aef6cd634afad8ea58ae/pkg/scheduler/framework/v1alpha1/waiting_pods_map.go#L41-L46

`PermitPlugin` plugin does not actually wait, it returns `Success` or `Wait` status codes (or `Error`, etc.), if `Wait` is returned then scheduler will create `WaitingPod` that can be allowed or rejected. 

Problem is that after permit plugin returns `Wait` status code, there are not guarantees when pod for which `Wait` was returned will be available as `WaitingPod` in the `FrameworkHandle`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b8e2b0d990ee0b780198aef6cd634afad8ea58ae/pkg/scheduler/framework/v1alpha1/framework.go#L779

I am describing a situation where 

1. Permit(podA) returns `Wait`
2. Before podA is added to `waitingPods` map Permit(podB) is called and allows waiting pods.
3. Then podA is added to `waitingPods` and never allowed.

This type of situation would not happen if we run Permit() in the scheduling cycle and create and add waitingPod to waitingPods there. Actual waiting on `<-waitingPod.s` can be done in the binding cycle.

In general, when you call `FrameworkHandle.GetWaitingPod(uid types.UID) WaitingPod` and get `nil` there can be 2 situations: 

1. pod was not added to the map yet
2. waiting pod was rejected

If Permit() and waitingPods update is serialized, then only situation 2. is possible, which is more predictable and less buggy.

I see the point.

Instead of separating the Permit extension point into two, is it possible to add a lock in the permit plugin implementation, so that the execution on pod A would block pod B? Per my understanding, why the racing issue can emerge is due to slight slow processing on pod A. In that case, moving Permit plugins to scheduling cycle wouldn't desirable as it would slow down the main scheduling loop.

I think lock will work as well to address this particular problem, but in my opinion running plugins in the scheduling cycle might be preferable because:

1. It guarantees the order in which permit plugins will be executed relative to other plugins. Consider for example situation where following happens: `reserve(podA), reserve(podB), ..., permit(podB), permit(podA)` in some cases it might lead to incorrect behavior (e.g. `permit(podB)` allowing waiting pods and them `permit(podA)` returning wait) unless there is some synchronization and state shared between pods. Personally I work on gang scheduling plugin and in general it would greatly simplify the logic I currently have in my code.
2. Explicitly locking in the binding cycle might be a little weird given that these goroutines were meant to run independently. If we are going to lock in the very beginning of the binding cycle, why not simply run that part in the scheduling cycle and guarantee the ordering in which permit() will be called?
3. Also as I mentioned earlier `FrameworkHandle.SnapshotSharedLister()` would be safe to use in permit plugins (though it would not have assumed pod).

I think this is a fair suggestion, we can split RunPermitPlugins into two phases:

1) RunPermitPlugins doesn't block and returns a Status and WaitingPod instance and is executed at the end of the scheduling cycle.
2) The WaitingPod [channel](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1c60045db0bd6efbb2827063e39f515b95c2bfa4/pkg/scheduler/framework/v1alpha1/waiting_pods_map.go#L84) should be buffered, a buffer of size one is sufficient.
3) The [waiting logic (L780-L793)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/v1alpha1/framework.go#L780-L793) in RunPermitPlugin is moved to a new framework function named ```WaitOnPermit```, and this new function is invoked in the binding cycle instead of RunPermitPlugins.

@ahg-g Why the channel should be buffered?

You can see initial draft here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88199.

> Why the channel should be buffered?

That doesn't sound necessary to me either.

@Huang-Wei Yes, I should have a bandwidth, I should have most of the PR ready today.

I really want this to make 1.18. Let me know how can I help.

> > Why the channel should be buffered?
> 
> That doesn't sound necessary to me either.

Because there could be a race between waiting and allowing/denying: 

1) podA returned wait and is added to the wait map
2) before the binding go routine of podA blocks on channel receive, podB scheduling cycle starts and it tries to allow/deny podA through a non blocking send
3) podA binding go routine blocks on channel receive, hence missing on podB's signal since it wasn't buffered

review_comments:
Main reason is that if we expose channel then we risk that custom plugin code will use `handle.GetWaitingPod(uid).StatusChan()` and intercept status that was meant for `WaitOnPermit()` and `WaitOnPermit()` will block forever. 

One option could be `Wait() *Status` or `Wait() (allowed bool)` which blocks until waiting pod is rejected or allowed and always return the same value that was memorized, however it would require more complicated `waitingPod` implementation. I think we should consider it as a separate feature and add it in the future if it is useful (right now it is not really possible to wait on a pod in the custom plugin code).

I decided to simply use `waitingPod` inside `waitingPodsMap` given that both types are internal and we do not need to use different implementation of the `WaitingPod` inside the `waitingPodsMap`. Also this way the framework API for the plugins does not change. In the future, if `waitingPodsMap` is exported type, then we will have to address it.
Using a concrete value here (instead of an interface) would lose the flexibility of building tests, but it's affordable. So SGTM.

There is quite a bit of repetition and inconsistency throughout the file in how we handle the errors. I think we should modify recordSchedulingFailure to accommodate all cases (e.g., which metric to increment, run unreserve or not, invoke ForgetPod or not etc.). I will do that in a follow up PR.
